9:50 you start talking about the 8GB VRAM that both the 3060 Ti and 6600 XT have and say these results in  Doom Eternal show what you feel more demanding future titles are going to look like on these GPUs, which I think is hilarious since for all the newer titles in your test suite, that's absolutely FALSE.  The premise is that the 3060 Ti is much better because of more memory bandwidth, but it's showing up in an OLDER title.

So, the current theory and you should already know this, if you haven't already said it, is using the highest quality settings in titles that these GPUs can run at really high frame rates is where the differences start to show.  Since Doom Eternal can run at very high fps, it's not as demanding.

So, Doom Eternal is certainly NOT indicative of what newer titles are going to look like for the differences between these 2 GPUs in newer titles, IF by what you mean is more textures which will slow down fps.  Games like RDR2 and Cyberpunk 2077 are better indicators of what these GPUs will look like in newer titles, since these are in fact, newer titles.

Clearly the 3060 Ti is a better GPU all around.  The fact that one game showed a much bigger gain for one GPU is basically meaningless since this happens all the time, and the titles will be different, and it can be driver based or a handful of other reasons.

comments.text:
I just bought this same card at Best Buy for US $320 (was a price matched deal). I've only had minimal time on it, but so far I think it's a rather good deal at this price range. These results are with no overclock and minimal tweaks beyond default settings, pci-e 3.0, using a 4k60 monitor.

I mainly play MSFS 2020, and this runs about 40-45 fps on the ground at O'Hare and around 50 fps in the air. This is on the medium graphics preset with render scaling at 80% (similar function as FSR and DLSS). For a flight sim, those are fine numbers because it's not fast acting and more about the visual beauty. The game looks great even though it's only at medium. I don't think it'll take much tweaking to get render scaling up to 85 with the same performance, at which point I don't even see a difference between it and full resolution at my viewing distance.

My other use is photo editing and I use several Topaz Labs programs which use the graphics card for processing too. In DeNoise AI, the preview updates very quick when panning and making adjustments that cause a re-rendering. Exporting a 24MP DNG file into a tiff takes 5 seconds on the built in timer, occasionally knocking one out in 4. Compare that to the longer preview updates and 20 second export times I was getting with the GTX 1060 3 GB card I replaced (2 minutes if using the CPU only) and working on 10-20 photos at a time, and this is a real time saver.

I was hoping to hold out for a 3080 ti, but that doesn't look to be in the cards for some time and this price was too attractive to pass up. My expectations were low, but I figured it would be an ok stop gap for now. It's been a surprisingly decent card, even on a 4k monitor. My only complaint is MSi Afterburner won't unlock power and voltage control for overclocking/undervolting. It may just need a reinstall due to the graphics card change, but haven't had time to really dig into that yet.

Okay guys, I have a bit of a bone to pick with an aspect of your reviews. Well two actually. Yes, I realize that this is months after the review was released, but it's still worth pointing out. Please note that I currently own a 6900XT, but previously I owned a pair of 1080Tis that I ran in SLI mode (well, tried to). So I am not an AMD fanboy; I will generally buy the best that's available, but given the size difference between AMD and its competitors, if the performance difference is less than 10 percent, I will go with the underdog, both for CPU and GPUs, and that's not taking price into account.  1) Why was it that although each game tested tends to get some level of development sponsorship from the various GPU manufacturers, the only game you point out specifically as getting AMD support is Assassin's Creed Valhalla? If you're going to call out who's bankrolling a title and has had opportunity to get low-level, device specific optimization specific to their respective hardware, then for each title, it's probably fair to call it out. If it's a TWIMTBP title, then it seems fair to call that out as well.  2) Secondly, and I've asked this before, why is it okay to test with DLSS optimization or Ray Tracing turned on (which clearly benefits Nvidia), but it's not okay to test with Resizable Bar turned on? It's almost like you're not playing each team's best players. 

Of course none of that detracts from the fact this card pretty much sucks, a conclusion I wholeheartedly agree with. I generally love your videos and make it a point of watching them, and I won't be so obnoxious to call you Nvidia biased- if anything their history has given you every reason not to be.

comments.text:
This is how I see this card, it is a 60 card, in both naming and in performance... Ill explain what that actually means.
When you look at AMD's line up, they have, starting at the bottom and going up, they have 40,50,60,70,80,90 video cards.  The 40 is just a card that allows the buyer to basically get to windows, but not really play games.  The 50 video card generally allows the buyer play games at super low quality.  The 60 video card allows the buyer to play games at what is considered the norm, which in our case right now that is 1080p at 60fps.   The 70 video card allows for higher settings in games, the 80 video card is considered high end, and the 90 video card is the top end.   This is how AMD's line up is set up, and its been this way for a while now.  Think about the RX-400 series of cards, followed by the RX-500 series cards, then there was of course the Vega line up that's kind of stand out, followed again by a stand alone card and then the 5000 series, and now the 6000 series.   The 6600xt is the 60 series card, which to give you a idea of where it is supposed to be priced in the line up of AMD video cards, the RX 460's MSRP was 86 dollars, the RX 560 was 99 dollars, and then we had the insane 5600xt which was 279 dollars, which was a huge jump in price when you think about it, and now the 6600xt's MSRP is 379..  
Looking at those prices, you can tell something changed between the RX-560 and the 5000 series video cards when it comes to pricing.  Inflation does not account for much of that price hike, Silicone being the second most abundant resource on our planet doesn't seem to be the likely problem ether.  You see, the price difference between the 460 and 560 can really be nothing but inflation, but the price difference in the 560 and the 5600 can not be just inflation.  After thinking about it, and looking at a bunch of pointless excuses and all out lies from not just AMD but NVIDIA and Intel alike, I realized what actually happened was nothing more than just greed of the people in charge of those company's, and a general ignorance on the consumers end. 
So should this video card be 200 dollars?  Nope, if we took the 86 dollars the RX 460 cost, and added inflation from then until now, the card would cost $97.82.. That means this card is actually nothing more than a sub 100 dollar video card, and they put a MSRP of 379 on it lol..   There are tons of Inflation calculators online that anyone can use for free, all you need to know is the year and the price of a object and you can see what the price would be now when you add inflation.

I, just like many others would love to see high performance GFX cards at extremely low prices. comments.text:
So, what Steve said at the end of the video about the availability of cards at MSRP on launch day came true, at least at my local Micro Center in the US.  The store had 200+ cards, mostly at or near the MSRP, on launch day, and the stock lasted through the entire day and part of the next.  But it does not look like this store, or any other retailer that I am aware of, re-supplied in any kind of significant quantity after launch day. 

eBay prices seem to be around $600-$650 currently and my guess this is where the prices will settle.  The prices of models on Micro Center's website have also trended higher with MSRP models not there anymore.  The most expensive ones are a $550 Strix and $560-570 MSI cards.  

It appears that the pattern for a couple of card launches has been having cards near MSRP available on launch day, but launch day only, and thereafter even the retail prices trend significantly up-- and in AMD AIB's cases, up enough to match eBay prices.  As Steve's charts show, this card at MSRP is much better value than 3060, 3060ti, etc. at secondary market prices.  So, the way to play this market is to absolute go buy a card on launch day at MSRP-- even if that MSRP doesn't look good compared to the MSRP of other cards, because the only launch day is about the only time you can get a card anywhere near the MSRP.

comments.text:
There were a few mistakes in the readouts:
- at Doom Eternal, rasterized @ 1440p, the difference to RX 5700 XT is 14/15%, not 19%
- at Doom Eternal, ray tracing, dropping from 288 FPS to 150 FPS is not an extreme 92% hit to the frame rate. Yeah, disabling RT would give 92% more frame rates, but computing the other way around, the hit to the frame rate would be 48%.

Given the above, can I personally ask to only provide the "X is faster than Y by Z%" or "X is slower than Y by Z%" in one video ? As in, only use faster or only use slower in one video, never both. Or if both, always have one of them presented. Also, I would vote for the "faster" approach. If you talk of 60% faster in one instance, then 10 seconds later on the next game you mention 60% slower, people don't realize what a MASSIVE difference that is. The "faster" numbers seem much better to show scale, I'd say. Ten times faster is 1000% (or +900%) performance which does look massive, while -90% performance doesn't.

And to play the devil's advocate (no, I'm not an AMD fanboy), maybe 6600 XT's MSRP, this time, IS adjusted to include the increase in components higher prices and tariffs and whatever else is affecting the price. In that hypothetical case, the MSRP would be actually useful and realistic, and if the rest of MSRP are adjusted to 2021's reality, it would compare much better. I guess that, as time goes by, we'll see if this is the case or not.

comments.text:
What the folks here and HU too seem to miss is that the market will mark up the prices anyway. AMD has no control over it. Even if it released the card at $1 MSRP, it would still be sold at ~500-600 USD. This means that you and HU asking for a lower official MSPR is useless and nonsense. 

Meanwhile by setting the MSRP higher AMD can at least somewhat keep up with the demand AND earn money themselves, not pass the profits onto scalpers and miners. This is logical. You, as consumers, will not be able to get the cards at MSRP anyway, so why give the profits to 3rd parties?

The only real solution to decreased prices is much higher supply - basically having AMD sell twice or thrice the amount of cards to drown the market with GPUs and make it unprofitable to scalp. However, AMD can’t do that because of limits to its own supply chain in wafers and other components. The critique on behalf of HU and the crowd isn’t warranted. As the host showed, AMD still is likely to succeed in its goal of making 6600XT the best GPU on cost/frame basis given MARKET prices

comments.text: This card has at least one cut too many, piled on the smaller die that's expected on a lower-end GPU: the 8 PCI lanes, the much smaller infinity cache, the anemic 128-bit bus. If just one of these three cuts was avoided this could be a well-balanced product, competitive in its category. While there's nothing wrong in having the entry-level of generation N have same performance of the high-end of gen N-1 such as the 5700 XT, you can't be wasted by your competitor at the same price range ($20 extra for the 3060 Ti = same price if you skip one McDonald's lunch). The only scenario where this product makes sense is good availability at MSRP or very close, since that would make it half the street price of its competition. But in a market where a new but two-generations-behind RX 580 8GB will cost more than those $379, I wouldn't hold my hopes high.

comments.text:
Something worth mentioning: rtx cards can run both. Also fsr truly shines at 4k when dropping below it starts to fall of a cliff, 1440p is just "fine" and 1080p is atrocious which makes perfect sense as its not really enhancing the image that much and its so limited in info relying on taa to create an image with enough info at such low resolutions. 

Dlss and even taa upscaling are called temporal upscalers which in layman's terms means they generate alot of info over frames (aka time) which is why they typically have a considerable amount of ghosting and blurring as they try to use previous frames to generate a great current frame along with current frame info anyways. Not having this extra info really isn't much of a deal breaker at higher resolutions outside incredibly cheap antialiasing (taa) as you have the info needed and hell 1440p already looks good as is so slightly improving 1662p looks great.

 A 1080p card means it has to at best case scenario it upscales 1080p higher but what it'll mean in future games is upscaling from say 720p. With this in mind fsr is more of a higher resolution upscaler (1440p+ starting)/makes rt work deal than dlss, there's alot of miss info out there and taa upscaling is what you should be talking about whether you like this answer or not, its a pill you have to swallow

comments.text: Worth pointing out as always that the "Texture Pool Size" setting in Doom Eternal simply specifies how much VRAM the game should use for pre-caching textures to reduce pop-in. There is no setting in Doom Eternal that allows for manually changing the resolution of the textures, though (which is tied directly to the actual resolution you're rendering the game at).

comments.text: 02:46  The cache has the same "bandwidth" (throughput is the correct term) as on other cards.  The numbers you're quoting are the effective throughput of the memory system, as measured by AMD.  That's the actual throughput of the memory controllers plus the effect of cache hits on the large L3 cache (i.e. "Infinity Cache").  The cache is smaller and the bus throughput is lower, so the effective overall throughput is also lower.

comments.text: @nahush6299  RX 6600 XT performs on average 15% faster than RTX 3060. Benchmarks by independent review websites like Tom's Hardware, TechRadar, PC Gamer and Eurogamer prove that. FSR works quite well at upscaling low resolution frames to higher resolution which enables it to game at 1080p with ray tracing. Plus FSR will be adopted more widely by developers than DLSS since it's open source and very easy to implement, plus it works on a much wider range of GPUs. RX 6600 XT doesn't require PCIe 4. The performance difference between PCIe 3 and PCIe 4 is very small as GPUs aren't that starved by PCIe bandwidth. RX 6600 XT is not crippled due to low memory bandwidth due to its Infinity Cache. Although RX 6600 XT has much less cores, it is very efficient in mining. Benchmarks have shown that its hash rate is 55 MH/s which is more than 3060 along with a lower power consumption. Even though it lacks Tensor Cores, RDNA 2 is very good in compute workloads which means it has great machine learning performance and it's encoder and decoder VCN 3.0 has been recently found to be more efficient than Nvidia's NVDEC and NVENC encoder and decoder respectively.

Simply because 3060Ti is a much bigger chip than 6600XT. 3060Ti will cost more to produce. 3060 is closer to 6600XT, but it is still a bit larger than 6600XT while also having 4GB more VRAM.
So it is not fair that the review insisted on comparing 6600XT to 3060Ti. I actually want to see the raytracing performance comparison between 6600XT and 3060 which unfortunately they didn't include. Comparing something at MSRP is fine as long as the MSRP is realistic.
If someone can actually sell 3060 and 3060Ti at MSRP, I'm pretty sure AMD WILL lower the price. It is just a basic business practice. Why in the world you expect AMD to launch 6600XT at closer to 3060 MSRP when you can't even find 3060 at MSRP? That is simply stupid business.

Of course at the end of the video they touched about the real world pricing, which honestly what I would expect (3060 and 3060Ti will be more expensive than 6600XT). The problem with that admission at the end is that they ended up with benchmark that comparing 6600XT with 3060Ti and ultimately using 3060Ti only for the raytracing comparison which is rather unfair. I don't expect 6600XT will have better raytracing performance vs 3060 (it isn't!) but I want to know how big the gap is between those card.

Also I read a lot about good will. Honestly, before talking about good will, people should realize the situation in the industry. Nvidia pricing 3060 that cheap is not because of goodwill but they simply using predatory pricing strategy. You ask people in the industry about Nvidia pricing for 3060 and they probably will say that it isn't realistic. Also the problem with the pricing strategy from Nvidia is that Nvidia want to push the losses to the card manufacturer, meaning that when Nvidia sold the chip, it is at the price where the manufacturer can't even produce the card to meet the MSRP at good quality.

What needs to happen is that we need to stop emphasizing on doing things because we can. Because we can produce a chip with 30billion transistor that doesn't mean we should if it can't be sold at a realistic price for most consumer. Right now I doubt low end pricing as we know before (like in $200 or lower) will be a thing for these new generation of GPU and instead we are simply moving like before, lower process node meaning higher transistor density, which unfortunately right now the new node doesn't actually bring cost saving so we ended up with the ever increasing price of chip that is produced using bleeding edge tech. What I'm sad that some PC elitist already declare that something like 3060 is a low end.... like.. seriously? The most popular card is 1060, and that card was $299. I doubt most people that are currently gaming with 1060 purchased that card at MSRP thus in reality, I wouldn't be surprised if most PC gamers can only afford a GPU significantly below $299. This is a market that these new GPUs haven't touch and probably will never touch and instead Nvida and AMD probably will keep raising the bar on not only performance but also price. The really sad thing is that most big reviewers simply doesn't care. They noticed that the price is getting higher, but most of them simply brush it aside and accept that 3070 is midrange and keep doing benchmark like everyone can afford an Ampere or RDNA2 cards. I'm not against reviewer review games using the most modern cards, what I don't like is that the reviewer think that is the most important metric... benchmarking game with Ampere only while the majority of gamers don't even have a raytracing capable GPU.

It seems that RDNA2 runs into scaling problems versus RDNA1 at lower CU and Infinity Cache counts.

Remember, AMD said that roughly 40% of the boost from RDNA1 to RDNA 2 was because of Infinity Cache, which only leaves 13% architecture-wise.

(Which sort of makes the PS5 and Series S|X sort of like RDNA "2" when comparing to the RDNA2 GPUs on PC as they don't have Infinity Cache)

And it seems that the 32CUs of RDNA2 roughly equates to 36 CUs of RDNA1 which is a 12.5% difference, so within the margin for that 13% base-arch boost outside of Infinity Cache.

Although if that is the case, unless if something is wrong with that card resulting in the scenarios where the 5700XT wins, then it seems Infinity Cache doesn't seem to work without specific memory bandwidth as I do feel the memory bandwidth is likely contributing to the diminished effectiveness of Infinity Cache in this card.

If this is the case, then that should make the leak about Lovelace having L3 Cache implemented per SM or per GPC at lower amounts but making it scale the L3 Cache as the GPC/SM count in the GPUs increase.


Running off Ampere's definition of a GPC being 12SMs, we can extrapolate potential Cache profiles for Lovelace (which ampere/Lovelace handle memory better than RDNA2, so even if the cache will be lower, it will wring more performance out per-cache Mb)
So for example, assuming an AD-104 die caps out at the same 48SMs of the GA-104 (for conjecture), then that would mean GPUs built on the range of 37-48SMs of Lovelace would have 4 GPCs, with that multiplied by how many mb of L3 cache per GPC NVIDIA assigns to Lovelace.

But this is a great video to make a point, which is how much to look at DATA and ignore all the commentary in the videos.  Pricing changes all the time if you haven't realized yet.  I've been building PCs since 1995 and the markets go through points of volatility where it's utterly useless to present information the way Steve did.  In fact it makes it hard for me to watch both HDWU and GN for this very reason.  The emphasis was a comparison between 2 theoretically "LIKE" products based on pricing that are both in current generations from their companies, Nvidia and AMD.

But the reality is the 3060 Ti has NEVER been priced close to the 6600 XT.  It's been as far as I watched over months, within about $150 - $200 of the 6600 XT.  So all the talk and bashing based on price was rubbish talk.  It wasn't REAL data.

I don't know what pricing is going to be like in 2 months because of how volitile the market is and there are too many issues making costs high.  Manufacturing costs have gone up about 20%, the biggest markets have large import taxes that didn't exist in 2020, transportation costs are higher, retailers are paying out more payroll for their employees, supply issues, etc....

What I know is right now I can buy a 6600 XT for about $500 USD.  I can't find a 3060 Ti for under $700 USD. You could say neither GPU is worth that price, but unfortunately that's the market now, and it's not AMD and Nvidia price gouging.  THAT is all the added cost right now.  The tariffs, inflation affecting everything I said above.  Most of the inflation is permanent, but the tariffs could go away and that would bring down cost about 20% which is a big deal.  That would make that $500 GPU $400 instead, over time, after new inventory entered countries.  For the US and Canadian market, if the ports could get all the workers they need and long haul trucking could get the drivers they need, companies could charge less for shipping, but the cost/container from China to the US has gone up quite a bit because ships are sitting off the coast of the US and they're losing money by having to sit, instead of moving more product.

So, very volatile market, pricing is changing, and the ONLY thing of value in this video was the comparison data.  I could have turned down the audio, stopped watching with about 8 minutes left and I would have gotten the only value this video has.  Even the intro had little value.

In other words, it makes not one bit of difference that pricing was brought up in the video, CLEARLY the market has been volatile since about Q4 of 2020 and pricing info in a video that's made at a single point in time is utterly worthless during such a time.  Just because a reviewer makes a comment, it doesn't make it valuable UNLESS it's hard data they're presenting, and when companies can't even predict what a valid MSRP is, clearly even MSRP isn't HARD data.  And even in times when the markets are stable, MSRP is a loose figure.  I shop AMD because of platform support over a few years as compared to Intel where a MB could be dead after one generation of CPUs.  Personal choice.  When people like Steve from HDWU and GN call a product "waste of sand", or "don't buy!" I go watch other reviews because I know I'm going to be listening to their propaganda piece, or I just look at their data and turn the sound down so I don't have to listen to their constant bashing or sarcasm.  I don't care what their opinions are because I can think for myself.  I want the data and nothing more.  They're going to talk about pricing, but at least for AMD, they will lower prices at some point, and it's usually near the next product release, and sometimes those discounts can be pretty big.  I bought a 5800X for $300 USD for a build.  I bought a 5600X for $210 USD for a build.  These products were BASHED because of their pricing, but I didn't pay those prices.  I don't care if GN and HDWU are unhappy because of GPU pricing.  EVERYONE is unhappy about GPU pricing.  What I care about is what I can buy when, and for how much.  All these comments on videos like this are utter rubbish because people are debating something that's constantly changing and in the case of this thread, just flat out wrong based on REAL pricing data.

The funny thing is, this GPU is now a 2K gaming GPU since RSR will work with almost every game.  And once FSR 2 is out and available in games, these "lower cost" GPUs are going to be much better value, very much in the same way DLSS 2 helps with lower end Nvidia GPUs.  I'm thankful these companies are doing the hard work to boost performance at ALL levels of their product stacks.  It makes a real difference.  I'll leave the hating on AMD and Nvidia to the uninformed masses.

@Scitch87  Well, I sold my GTX 1070 for £300, and bought an ASUS 6600 xt on release day for £380.

There is also SAM which can give up to a 15% performance increase. 
When I was playing AC: Valhalla for the last couple of months, I already had a massive gain over the RTX 3060, and when I enabled SAM in the Bios I got another 15%.

That's an insane difference, especially since the 6600 xt is still cheaper than the RTX 3060 in the UK.

comments.text:
This is how I see this card, it is a 60 card, in both naming and in performance... Ill explain what that actually means.
When you look at AMD's line up, they have starting at the bottom and going up, they have 40,50,60,70,80,90 video cards.  The 40 is just a card that allows the buyer to basically get to windows, but not really play games.  The 50 video card generally allows the buyer play games at super low quality.  The 60 video card allows the buyer to play games at what is considered the norm, which in our case right now that is 1080p at 60fps.   The 70 video card allows for higher settings in games, the 80 video card is considered high end, and the 90 video card is the top end.   This is how AMD's line up is set up, and its been this way for a while now.  Think about the RX-400 series of cards, followed by the RX-500 series cards, then there was of course the Vega line up that kind of stand out, followed again by a stand alone card and then the 5000 series, and now the 6000 series.   The 6600xt is the 60 series card, which to give you a idea of where it is supposed to be priced in the line up of AMD video cards, the RX 460's MSRP was 86 dollars, the RX 560 was 99 dollars, and then we had the insane 5600xt which was 279 dollars, which was a huge jump in price when you think about it, and now the 6600xt's MSRP is 379..  
Looking at those prices, you can tell something changed between the RX-560 and the 5000 series video cards when it comes to pricing.  Inflation does not account for much of that price hike, Silicone being the second most abundant resource on our planet doesn't seem to be the likely problem ether.  You see, the price difference between the 460 and 560 can really be nothing but inflation, but the price difference in the 560 and the 5600 can not be just inflation.  After thinking about it, and looking at a bunch of pointless excuses and all out lies from not just AMD but NVIDIA and Intel alike, I realized what actually happened was nothing more than just greed of the people in charge of those company's, and a general ignorance on the consumers end. 
So should this video card be 200 dollars?  Nope, if we took the 86 dollars the RX 460 cost, and added inflation from then until now, the card would cost $97.82.. That means this card is actually nothing more than a sub 100 dollar video card, and they put a MSRP of 379 on it lol..   There are tons of Inflation calculators online that anyone can use for free, all you need to know is the year and the price of a object and you can see what the price would be now when you add inflation.  
So how much should this video card be?  Well, Id buy one for 100 dollars, that is just slightly above what it should be, but not a penny higher...
